title: Spatiotemporal Variability of Water Transit Time Distribution Across an Alpine Stream Network
content:
Abstract

Water transit time (TT), the time elapsed from its entrance into a catchment and its exit through a stream section, is a useful indicator of catchment transport dynamics. Its distribution (TTD) is typically estimated at a single cross section where tracer data are available. However, spatial variability of TTD is key to understanding how heterogeneous source areas contribute to solute and water quality dynamics. Here, we investigate how TTD varies along a stream network. To this end, we analyzed stable isotopes in rainfall (three stations) and streamwater (eight sampling sites) in the Valfredda network draining an alpine catchment. To quantitatively analyze the data, we developed a spatially explicit model of TTD based on StorAge Selection (SAS) functions. The catchment is discretized into subcatchment units, each characterized by distinct SAS functions. Subcatchment TTDs are routed through the network to estimate TTDs at every cross section. Parameter estimation relies on a hierarchical Bayesian framework, which ensures consistency across subcatchments while allowing heterogeneity. Results indicate that streamflow preferentially samples older water from storage, with only a limited number of flow events triggering young water release. Despite pronounced heterogeneity in geomorphology and land cover, the inferred SAS functions exhibit only mild spatial variability. Differences in TTDs are driven primarily by variations in precipitation phase (liquid vs. solid) and the timing of snowmelt-driven fluxes, rather than by intrinsic differences in mixing mechanisms. Both sources of variability are explicitly represented within the proposed framework, highlighting its general applicability to reveal transport dynamics at the catchment scale.
